tags.gist: Recommends three separate assurance layers, competency testing, clinical confirmation and operational assurance, since benchmark results alone cannot assure safety.
Proposes three assurance layers, competency, clinical confirmation and operational assurance, and says no layer can replace another.
Calls the two-axis framework insufficient, since activity does not equal probability of harm, and would use standard probability-and-severity hazard analysis with risk controls.
Would let reversibility, time pressure, traceability and safeguards modify the risk analysis, without adding more graphical axes.
Would replace grading by wording with one division, general versus patient-specific output, treating patient-specific output as potentially action-directing.
Accepts professional review as reducing residual risk only if the manufacturer proves the control effective, including against automation bias.
Agrees patient-facing devices can carry more risk when patients cannot assess outputs, while not assuming patients lack capability.
Lists patient-facing controls: limited scope, clear sources, uncertainty information, human review before high-consequence actions, escalation, and tests across users and long conversations.
Wants users giving false information or bypassing safety controls treated as foreseeable and included in the risk analysis.
Suggests monitoring interactions to flag high-risk conversations for human review, possibly by a second AI that must itself be tested and monitored.
Says risk rises where safe use requires specialist knowledge the user lacks, and treats specialist and generalist devices as different devices to confirm separately.
Lists controls such as verified roles, role-based access, specialist confirmation and automatic deferral, using verified role data rather than inferring specialty.
Wants complete conversations assessed, including long sessions, boundary-crossing attempts, fictional framing, conflicting information, memory and repeated runs.
Would use deterministic filters outside the model for measurable scope boundaries such as age, role, domain and permitted actions, as current devices do.
Says out-of-scope behavior that no control stops must be treated as foreseeable and included in the safety evaluation.
Adds a third error type, failed escalation, where the handoff goes to the wrong service, arrives late or is not acted on.
Lists escalation measures: sensitivity, error rates, time to escalation, destination, handoff completion and clinical result.
Wants severe under-escalation to have its own pass-or-fail limit that good performance on common cases cannot offset.
Calls the competency approach necessary, requires testing the final configuration with all components, and treats benchmarking as a gate rather than full assurance.
Wants a separate acceptance limit for each high-consequence failure, since an average score can hide one.
Lists competency tests from omissions and scope control to tool use, unauthorized actions and post-change behavior, each mapped to intended use or a hazard.
Wants sponsors to show representative and rare cases, prespecified limits, held-out data, independent review, stable repeats and clinical support for benchmark results.
Says the amount of evidence should follow hazard analysis and control effectiveness, not the two-axis framework directly.
Says the three-layer approach fits multimodal and world models, adding tests for cross-modal mismatches, multi-step error and counterfactuals; the final device stays the unit.
Sees a master file as useful dependency information, not proof of safety, listing contents from version and failure modes to rollback and withdrawal plans.
Says a voluntary master file can reduce repeated work, but another method should be required where the provider withholds sufficient information.
Wants agentic devices assessed for wrong plans, compounding errors, wrong tools, unauthorized actions, prompt injection, privilege escalation and failure to stop or reverse.
Wants least privilege, deterministic tool and action limits, human approval for high-consequence actions, full logs, a stop control and rollback, with permissions matched to function.
Would pick the confirmation method by harm and uncertainty: retrospective for narrow objective tasks, shadow for local effects, prospective for irreversible actions, multi-site where needed.
Wants a defined unit of analysis, clustering handled, repeated runs to measure variation, stratified reporting, and synthetic, real and benchmark results kept separate.
Finds synthetic data useful for scope, rare hazards and adversarial tests but not for communication, behavior or outcomes; wants an independent generator and real-data confirmation.

Would compare against care as it would happen without the device, including current software, measuring safety, time to care, workload and subgroup differences.
Gives third parties roles from holding hidden test data to auditing monitoring, with expertise, conflict disclosure, multiple qualified bodies and continued manufacturer accountability.
Allows more premarket uncertainty only with limited deployment, fallback, version records, alert limits, named reviewers and rollback, never for irreversible or undetectable harm.
Wants monitoring across system operation, input quality, performance, human-device interaction and outcomes, including overrides and automation bias.
Wants random plus risk-based review and a specified action for every signal; a dashboard with no action process is not a control.
Accepts machine supervisors for case selection if tested as safety components, built on a different model family, backed by deterministic controls and sampled by humans.
Keeps the manufacturer accountable, assigns local roles to providers and clinicians, and suggests FDA back a confidential monitoring network across sites.
Would classify changes by effect: quality-system control for low-effect, PCCPs for bounded prompt, retrieval and guardrail changes, and FDA review for material changes.
Wants contracts giving notice, versions, deprecation periods and rollback, plus technical controls such as pinned versions and regression tests, with full reassessment after changes.
Concludes with three assurance layers, a general-versus-patient-specific division instead of wording, deterministic boundary controls and action-linked monitoring signals.
